title: Newton's Method
subtitle: Using tangent lines to home in on a root

slides.title: Newton's Method
slides.text:
Newton's method has one job: **finding roots**.
A root of $f$ is an $x$-value where $f(x)$ = 0. On a graph, it is where the curve crosses the $x$-axis.
Tap one of the roots of this function.
slides.howto: Tap the graph right where the curve crosses the $x$-axis.
slides.hint: Look for a spot where the curve meets the horizontal axis.
slides.explain: Right. This curve crosses the axis at $x$ = −2 and at $x$ = 3. (Factoring gives the same thing: $(x - 3)(x + 2)$ = 0.)

slides.title: Now a hard one
slides.text:
$f(x)$ = $x^5 + 8x^4 + 4x^3 - 2x - 7$
There is no formula for the roots of a fifth-degree polynomial (nothing like the quadratic formula), and this one will not factor. But we can still **see** a root.
Tap roughly where the **positive** root is.
slides.howto: Tap the graph where the curve crosses the $x$-axis to the right of 0.
slides.hint: The positive root is to the right of $x$ = 0. Find where the curve crosses the axis there.
slides.explain: Good eye: the root is near $x$ = 0.9. But seeing it is not the same as knowing it to six decimal places, and we cannot solve for it. We need a way to **approximate** it.

slides.text: Between which two whole numbers is the positive root?
slides.hint: Find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis to the right of 0.
slides.explain: The curve crosses between 0 and 1. Check the signs: $f(0)$ = −7 is negative and $f(1)$ = 4 is positive.

slides.title: How do we know?
slides.text: $f(0)$ = −7 is negative and $f(1)$ = 4 is positive. Which theorem guarantees that $f$ has a root somewhere between 0 and 1?
slides.hint: $f$ is a polynomial, so it is continuous, and it goes from negative to positive. Which theorem says a continuous function takes on every value in between?
slides.explain: The **Intermediate Value Theorem**. $f$ is continuous on [0, 1], and 0 is between $f(0)$ = −7 and $f(1)$ = 4, so $f(c)$ = 0 for some $c$ between 0 and 1. The theorem says a root is there, but not exactly where. Newton's method will find it.

slides.title: Idea: follow the tangent line
slides.text:
Make a guess, $x_0$ = 1.3. Close to that point, the curve looks a lot like its tangent line, and a line is easy to solve.
Here is the tangent line at $x_0$. **Tap where it crosses the $x$-axis.** That spot is the next guess, $x_1$.
slides.howto: Follow the dashed tangent line down to the $x$-axis and tap there.
slides.hint: Follow the dashed line (not the curve) until it meets the horizontal axis.
slides.explain: That is $x_1$ ≈ 1.05. It is much closer to the root (near 0.90) than $x_0$ = 1.3 was. Do it again from $x_1$ and you get closer still.

slides.title: Try it, one piece at a time
slides.text: Same function. Pick a first guess $x_0$. Then **draw the tangent line** and **tap where it crosses the $x$-axis**: that is $x_1$. Repeat from $x_1$. Use **Zoom +** to see how close you are. Keep going until the digits stop changing.
slides.after: The root is about {x}. You found it in {n} steps. Notice how fast the digits settle once you are close.

slides.text: In Newton's method, where does the next guess $x_1$ come from?
options: Where the tangent line at $x_0$ crosses the $x$-axis
slides.hint: Think about what you just did with the slider.
slides.explain: Draw the tangent line at $x_0$; it crosses the $x$-axis at $x_1$.

slides.title: Turn the picture into a formula
slides.text:
The tangent line at $x_0$ passes through the point $(x_0, f(x_0))$ and has slope $f'(x_0)$.
We want the spot where this line hits the $x$-axis.

Point-slope form of the tangent line:
y − ___ = ___ (x − x₀)
slides.hint: Point-slope form is $y - y_1$ = $m(x - x_1)$. The point is $(x_0, f(x_0))$ and the slope is the derivative.

slides.text: On the x-axis, y = ___. And the x-value where the line hits the axis is our new guess, ___.
slides.hint: Every point on the $x$-axis has the same $y$-value.

slides.text: Start from  0 − f(x₀) = f′(x₀)(x₁ − x₀).  Divide both sides by ___ .
slides.hint: We want $x_1 - x_0$ by itself. What is it multiplied by?

slides.explain: Add $x_0$ to both sides. The minus sign stays with the fraction.

slides.title: Newton's Method
slides.text:
First step:  $x_1$ = $x_0 - frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}$
Then do it again from $x_1$ to get $x_2$, and so on. In general:
$x_n$ = $x_(n-1) - frac{f(x_(n-1))}{f'(x_(n-1))}$
New guess = old guess minus $f$ over $f'$, both at the old guess.

Fill in the formula:
xₙ = ___ − frac{___}{___}
slides.hint: Everything on the right side is at the old guess, $x_(n-1)$. Value on top, derivative on the bottom.

slides.title: Let it run
slides.text: Here is $f(x)$ = $x^3 - 3x + 1$, starting at $x_0$ = 0. Tap **Next guess** a few times and watch the table. How many steps until the digits stop changing?
slides.after: Settled at {x} after {n} steps. Already $x_3$ matched the root to 6 decimal places.

slides.title: More than root finding
slides.text:
Newton's method can also compute numbers like √2.
The trick: write down a function whose root **is** the number you want. Then find that root.
Which function has √2 as a root?
slides.hint: Plug in $x$ = √2 and see which one gives 0.

slides.text: Watch the guesses close in on √2.
slides.after: √2 ≈ {x} after {n} steps. A calculator says √2 = 1.41421356… Just three steps gave five correct decimal places.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
**Newton's method:** guess, slide down the tangent line to the $x$-axis, repeat.
$x_n$ = $x_(n-1) - frac{f(x_(n-1))}{f'(x_(n-1))}$
It usually homes in on a root in just a few steps. Does it always work? You will find out in the theory drill.

questions.text: Newton's method is a way to approximate…
options: the maximum value of a function
the slope of a tangent line

questions.text: Newton's method usually gives the exact root after one step.
questions.explain: One step gives an approximation. Repeating the step makes it better and better.

questions.text: The tangent line at $x_0$ is drawn. Which labeled point is $x_1$?
questions.explain: $x_1$ is where the **tangent line** crosses the $x$-axis (C). B is the actual root, which $x_1$ only approximates.

questions.text: To get x₁, draw the ___ line at x₀ and find where it crosses the ___.
questions.explain: Follow the tangent line at $x_0$ down to the $x$-axis.

questions.text: Which is Newton's formula?
We start Newton's method for $f(x)$ = $x^3 - 3x + 1$ at $x_0$ = 1. What goes wrong?
options: The tangent line is flat, so it never crosses the $x$-axis
Nothing; it finds the root near 0.347
Nothing; it finds the root near 1.532
It gives $x_1$ = 1, which is a root
questions.explain: $f'(1)$ = 3 − 3 = 0. The tangent is horizontal ($y$ = −1) and the formula would divide by zero.

questions.text: If $f'(x_0)$ = 0, Newton's formula divides by zero, so it cannot produce $x_1$.
questions.explain: The formula has $f'(x_0)$ in the denominator.

questions.text: If $f'(x_0)$ = 0, what does the tangent line at $x_0$ look like?
options: Horizontal, so it never meets the $x$-axis (unless $f(x_0)$ = 0)
Exactly the same as the curve
questions.explain: Slope 0 means a horizontal line. Picture: a flat tangent at the bottom of a valley.

questions.text: $f'(x_0)$ is very close to 0, but not 0. What usually happens to $x_1$?
options: It lands exactly on the root
questions.explain: A nearly flat tangent crosses the axis far away. Dividing by a tiny $f'(x_0)$ makes a huge jump.

questions.text: Newton's method always finds a root, no matter where you start.
questions.explain: It can fail: a flat tangent, guesses that run away, or guesses that bounce back and forth forever.

questions.text: For a smooth function, if $x_0$ is close enough to a root, the guesses usually close in on that root very quickly.
questions.explain: Near the root the curve looks like its tangent line, so each step lands very close. (It needs $f'$ not to be 0 at the root.)

questions.text: For $f(x)$ = $x^3 - 2x + 2$ starting at $x_0$ = 0, Newton's method gives $x_1$ = 1 and then $x_2$ = 0. What happens if you keep going?
options: The guesses bounce between 0 and 1 forever and never reach a root
The guesses close in on a root
questions.explain: $x_2$ is back where we started, so the pattern repeats: 0, 1, 0, 1, … This is a cycle.

questions.text: To approximate √5 with Newton's method, use which function?
To approximate the cube root of 10, use which function?
questions.explain: The cube root of 10 is a root of $x^3 - 10$.

questions.text: To solve $cos x$ = $x$, apply Newton's method to which function?
questions.explain: Move everything to one side: $cos x - x$ = 0. Its root solves the equation.
The fraction is $0/f'(x_0)$ = 0. You are already at a root, so you stay there.

questions.text: If $f(x_0)$ > 0 and $f'(x_0)$ > 0, then $x_1$ is to the left of $x_0$.
questions.explain: $frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}$ is positive, and we subtract it, so we move left. The curve is above the axis and rising, so the root is behind us.
The fraction is negative, and subtracting a negative moves right. Below the axis and rising: the root is ahead.

questions.text: What does Newton's method need from $f$?
questions.explain: Each step uses $f'$, so $f$ needs a derivative there. It works on trig, exponential and other functions too.

questions.text: The tangent line at $x_0$ is drawn. Where will $x_1$ be?
questions.explain: Follow the tangent line to the $x$-axis: it crosses to the right of $x_0$. (Here $f(x_0)$ < 0 and $f'(x_0)$ > 0, so we subtract a negative and move right.) It overshoots the root, but the next step comes back.

questions.text: Newton's method breaks down right away if you start at which labeled point?
questions.explain: At Q the curve bottoms out (a local min), so the tangent line there is flat: $f'(x_0)$ = 0. A flat tangent never reaches the $x$-axis, and the formula would divide by zero.

questions.text: For $f(x)$ = $x^3 - 2x + 2$, the tangent at $x_0$ = 0 leads to $x_1$ = 1, and the tangent at $x_1$ leads back to 0. What happens?
options: The guesses bounce between 0 and 1 forever and never reach the root
The guesses close in on the root near −1.77
The tangent line is flat, so it stops
questions.explain: The two tangent lines send each guess back to the other one: 0, 1, 0, 1, … The real root is near −1.77, but Newton's method never gets there from this start.

questions.text: The tangent line at $x_0$ = 2 is drawn for $f(x)$ = $x^3 - x - 1$. Tap where $x_1$ is.
questions.howto: Follow the dashed tangent line down to the $x$-axis and tap there.
questions.explain: $x_1$ is where the tangent line (not the curve) crosses the $x$-axis: $x_1$ = $2 - frac{5}{11}$ ≈ 1.545.

questions.text: Newton's method: $x_0$ = 3, $f(3)$ = 2 and $f'(3)$ = 4. Find $x_1$.
Newton's method: $x_0$ = 1, $f(1)$ = −3 and $f'(1)$ = 6. Find $x_1$.
Newton's method: $x_0$ = 2, $f(2)$ = 5 and $f'(2)$ = −2. Find $x_1$.
Newton's method: $x_0$ = −1, $f(−1)$ = 4 and $f'(−1)$ = 8. Find $x_1$.
Newton's method: $x_0$ = 0, $f(0)$ = 1 and $f'(0)$ = −4. Find $x_1$.
Newton's method: $x_0$ = 4, $f(4)$ = −2 and $f'(4)$ = 0.5. Find $x_1$.
Newton's method: $x_0$ = −2, $f(−2)$ = −6 and $f'(−2)$ = 9. Find $x_1$.
Newton's method: $x_0$ = 2, $f(2)$ = 3 and $f'(2)$ = 0. Find $x_1$.
questions.explain: $f'(x_0)$ = 0, so the formula divides by zero: the tangent line is flat.

questions.text: $f(x)$ = $x^2 - 5$, starting at $x_0$ = 2. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $x^3 - 10$, starting at $x_0$ = 2. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $x^3 + x - 1$, starting at $x_0$ = 1. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $x^2 - 3x + 1$, starting at $x_0$ = 3. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $cos x - x$, starting at $x_0$ = 1. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $x^7 + 4$, starting at $x_0$ = −1. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $frac{2}{x} - x^2 + 1$, starting at $x_0$ = 2. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $x^4 - 2$, starting at $x_0$ = 1. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $e^x - 3$, starting at $x_0$ = 1. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $sin x$, starting at $x_0$ = 3. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $ln x - 1$, starting at $x_0$ = 3. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
$f(x)$ = $x^2 - 4$, starting at $x_0$ = 0. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
questions.explain: $f'(x)$ = $2x$, and $f'(0)$ = 0. The tangent line is flat, so the formula divides by zero.

questions.text: $f(x)$ = $x^3 - 3x + 1$, starting at $x_0$ = 1. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
questions.explain: $f'(x)$ = $3x^2 - 3$, and $f'(1)$ = 0. The tangent line is flat, so the formula divides by zero.

questions.text: $f(x)$ = $x^3 - 12x + 3$, starting at $x_0$ = 2. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
questions.explain: $f'(x)$ = $3x^2 - 12$, and $f'(2)$ = 0. The tangent line is flat, so the formula divides by zero.

questions.text: $f(x)$ = $cos x$, starting at $x_0$ = 0. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
questions.explain: $f'(x)$ = $-sin x$, and $f'(0)$ = 0. The tangent line is flat, so the formula divides by zero.

questions.text: $f(x)$ = $x^3 - 6x^2 + 5$, starting at $x_0$ = 4. Give decimals to at least 3 places.
questions.explain: $f'(x)$ = $3x^2 - 12x$, and $f'(4)$ = 0. The tangent line is flat, so the formula divides by zero.
